In Wisner (Dasyscopelus selenops), hatchlings emerge from pelagic eggs with an extremely modest body mass, with newly eclosed yolk-sac larvae weighing approximately 0.00052 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00052 grams]. This minute initial size, typical of many myctophids, reflects a life-history strategy reliant on high fecundity and rapid early growth in the productive upper layers of the water column. The first exogenous feeding occurs shortly after yolk-sac resorption, marking a critical trophic switch for the developing larva. As these larvae progress through the pre-metamorphic and flexion stages, they accumulate somatic tissue rapidly, and by the time of the larval-juvenile transition, individuals have substantially increased in mass. Field surveys and growth-curve estimations from otolith increment analysis suggest that the ultimate wet weight attained by adults is approximately 4.2 grams [Wwi = approximately 4.2 grams], a value that corresponds to the asymptotic maximum recorded in field-sampled specimens. This adult mass is consistent with the general size range observed among mesopelagic lanternfishes of similar standard lengths, indicating that Dasyscopelus selenops occupies a typical trophic position within its community.

At this developmental stage, the wet weight at puberty is approximately 1.2 grams [Wwp = approximately 1.2 grams], which aligns well with the predicted mass derived from length-weight relationships for this species. This relatively small size at maturity suggests that resources are allocated toward reproduction early in the life cycle, a common trait among myctophids that operate in an environment where predation pressure is high and adult survivorship is unpredictable. The length at full adulthood, representing the ultimate standard length, has been recorded at 7.5 centimeters [Li = 7.5 centimeters], indicating that significant somatic growth continues after the onset of reproductive activity. This decoupling of size at puberty from ultimate size implies a protracted period of post-maturation mass accumulation.

Reproductive investment in Dasyscopelus selenops is substantial and has been characterized through analysis of ovarian condition and spawning frequency. Under the ambient thermal conditions of its habitat, a stable water temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C] is typical for much of the spawning season. At this temperature, the maximum reproductive rate is achieved through a combination of high spawning frequency and moderate clutch sizes. Females produce approximately 6.3 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 6.3 eggs per spawning event] and can complete roughly one spawning episode per day [F_R_i = roughly one spawning episode per day] during the most favorable months. This daily spawning schedule is unusual among myctophids and indicates a remarkably rapid oocyte turnover, likely fueled by the reliable availability of zooplanktonic prey in the productive waters where this species aggregates. The total daily output represents a significant energetic investment relative to the female's body mass, underscoring the species' capacity for high population turnover despite the small size of individual recruits.

The lifespan of Dasyscopelus selenops has been determined from mark-recapture studies and validated by otolith-based aging of wild-caught individuals. Under the consistently cool thermal regime of its mesopelagic environment, maintained at 17 °C [T = 17 °C] in the upper portion of its depth range, maximum recorded longevity reaches approximately 1,095 days [am = approximately 1,095 days]. This comparatively short lifespan is typical of small, fast-growing myctophids that experience high rates of natural mortality from predators including larger fish, squid, and marine mammals. The three-year maximum constrains the total number of reproductive opportunities available to an individual female, amplifying the selective importance of the high daily fecundity observed in this species. By reproducing nearly daily over most of its adult life, an individual can potentially produce more than six thousand eggs across its lifetime, a strategy that buffers against the very low survival probabilities of the pelagic larval stage. This near-isometric growth pattern is common among small mesopelagic fishes that maintain a streamlined, fusiform body shape throughout ontogeny. Comparisons with congeneric species reveal that Dasyscopelus selenops exhibits a relatively high mass at a given length, possibly reflecting a greater investment in energy-dense tissues such as lipid stores, which would aid in buoyancy control and fasting endurance during periods of low prey availability in the deep scattering layer.
